section.title: Ryan and Ricky: Internships, Promotions, and Big Tech vs Startups
section.deck: Ryan and Ricky argue that visible work, frequent questions, and clear writing shape early careers as much as coding skill, and they compare big tech with startups.

blocks.text: Ryan and Ricky, who both studied at UCLA, share what they wish they had known before graduating. Ryan manages interns at Meta, and Ricky works on ads at Google. Their central view is that early career progress depends on visible impact, frequent questions, and clear writing, more than on coding skill or luck alone. They also explain engineering levels, how interns are judged, how to earn a promotion, and how to weigh big tech against startups. The talk then covers money, job changes, and AI's effect on entry-level work. These are the speakers' own views and experience, not general rules.
blocks.heading: The speakers' view: visible work, questions, and writing shape early careers

blocks.question: What do the engineering levels mean, from junior to staff?
answer: Ricky explains that junior engineers write and ship code with a fair amount of help. Mid-level engineers work more independently but still need help at times. Senior is often a stopping point, with few people expected to go further. Staff engineers set a team's direction and lead engineers at other levels. Ricky estimates that moving from junior to mid-level takes about two to four years, and mid-level to senior a similar time.

Ricky says some companies use an up-or-out policy, where people who do not reach the next level leave, and that Google is less aggressive about this. Ricky estimates, without exact data, that 90 percent or more of people reach these levels. The speakers say the levels site is fairly accurate, except that equity pay moves with the stock price.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How do interns succeed, and how are they judged?
answer: The speakers say interns are judged on three things. The first is productivity: how much of the assigned project they finish, ideally in half the internship. The second is quality, shown by fewer rounds of code review by the end. The third is communication, including proposing improvements or a new project after finishing the first one. A strong intern does all three.

followups.question: What was Ricky's own internship like?
answer: Ricky's junior-year internship at Google produced only about 800 lines of code, which felt low. Halfway through, Ricky had about 300 lines, while a UCLA friend on the same program had about 11,000. Ricky spent much of the time learning the codebase and wrote a detailed design doc comparing several approaches. That work showed productivity, and Ricky received a return offer.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How did you get promoted so quickly to staff engineer in your 20s?
answer: Ricky says each level expects a different kind of work. Many projects at the current level do not earn the next promotion. One project at the next level, which clearly shows readiness, counts for more. Managers often describe these expectations as behaviors. Ricky and Ryan focused on projects that would move them up, not on busy work that would not.

Ricky also says that, after each promotion, Ricky asked the manager what the next level required and then took on that kind of work. The manager explained which skills to build, and Ricky credits this for the fast promotions.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Is career success mostly luck?
answer: Ryan says luck is a big part of it, but people can raise their own luck through initiative. After about eight months at Amazon, Ryan felt stuck and could not see the path to the next level. Ryan applied to many companies and received offers from every company interviewed with except one. That led to Meta.

followups.question: Is luck mostly opportunity, or can preparation change the outcome?
answer: Ryan adds that grinding LeetCode problems and applying widely raised the odds, and that personal agency matters. Ricky frames luck as two parts: the opportunity itself, and being prepared when it comes. Without preparation, a good chance can pass by. Ricky adds that Ryan's move away from Amazon created more opportunities.

blocks.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: What one piece of advice would the speakers give?
answer: Ricky says the main advice is to ask a lot of questions, at work and during an internship. Ricky once told a mentee to keep asking, and at the end of the internship the mentee said Ricky had not really meant it. Ricky says the biggest difference between people who succeed quickly and those who do not is how fast they start asking questions, learning, and unblocking themselves. Fear of looking foolish holds many people back.

followups.question: What separates strong interns from weak ones?
answer: Ryan has had five interns at Meta. The strong ones had the nerve to propose improvements and ask questions, even though Ryan was the senior person. Some suggestions were wrong, but many were right. The weaker interns were quieter, and Ryan could not tell how they were progressing. Time passed with little progress, and such interns often did not get return offers.
followups.speaker: Ryan

blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Are the best engineers the smartest students in the class?
answer: The speakers say no. Strong engineers need solid technical skill and soft skills, such as persuading and influencing others. Work is a large group project, and disagreements are common. Telling a colleague that their idea is bad does not win them over. Naming the other person's frustration, acknowledging their view, and proposing a middle ground makes it more likely that the work ships. The speakers say these skills matter about as much as coding.

blocks.question: How much of the job is actually code?
answer: One speaker says code is a smaller part of the job than new graduates expect. Writing is a large part of it. A design doc comes before the code, a change needs a written description, and a finished project needs a write-up of its results. The speaker says this writing is how a person influences others, so people skills often decide how far an engineer goes.

blocks.question: Do experienced engineers still get imposter syndrome?
answer: Ricky says imposter syndrome is very common, and that most people feel it. Ricky felt it on joining Google, after passing the interviews and the internship, and found the other engineers very strong. Even after promotions, Ricky wondered whether the company had made a mistake. Ricky copes by learning as much as possible and doing the best job possible, on the view that even being fired would leave something learned. Ricky says the feeling still returns in waves.

followups.question: Did praise at work reduce the stress?
answer: Ricky describes being an anxious person who was always stressed about work. A manager once told Ricky to calm down. Ricky was not sure whether the praise meant a passing grade or a strong one. Talking through expectations with the manager helped, and the stress eased somewhat.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: How do you advocate for yourself at work?
answer: Ryan says good work is required but not enough, because people decide promotions and they must know about the work. The last few percent of effort is to tell people about it. That can mean writing about a result, presenting it in a meeting, or telling a manager that a milestone is done early and the next task is ready. Ryan says a clear post about strong results makes a return offer hard to refuse. Ryan says this step is often skipped, especially by introverted people.

followups.question: Is visibility a separate skill from doing the work?
answer: Ricky says visibility can come from a manager, a product manager, or teammates, as well as from the person's own writing. Ricky compares unseen work to a tree falling in a forest that nobody sees, and says people cannot promote work they do not know about.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: Should new graduates choose big tech or a startup?
answer: The room was polled first. Most audience members chose big tech. Those who chose startups cited first-mover upside and a larger share of impact at a smaller company. Ryan says big tech brings brand value, so a resume from a known company is an easier hire. Ryan describes Amazon as the lowest tier of the big companies at the time, yet recruiter messages arrived in large numbers after joining it.

Ryan frames the choice as a trade-off between high expected value and high variance. Big tech usually gives a better average outcome on a steady path, but rarely produces very large wealth. A startup can boom or fail. Someone who joins early and the company grows can rise quickly, which big tech rarely allows.

followups.question: Why did Ricky choose big tech over startup offers?
answer: Ricky had offers from both startups and big tech, and chose big tech for work-life balance. Ricky's startup friends work very hard, and the results have varied. Ricky says big tech teaches established practices with less variance, while a startup's role can change a lot. Ricky recommends big tech, at least for the first few years, to build prestige and a base.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: How do managers measure impact?
answer: The speakers define impact as the concrete, measurable results of the work, such as revenue, cost, speed, or user growth. The measure depends on the team. On an ads team it may be money. On infrastructure it may be the cost or latency of a database. On a growth team it may be daily active users or sign-ups at key steps. Engineers should learn the measure from their team and manager, because that is how their work is rewarded.

The speakers also say one small change that improves a key number can matter more than ten thousand lines of typo fixes. Their example is a one-line change that gives a 20 percent gain on something that matters.

blocks.question: Do you need an MBA for engineering management?
answer: Ryan says no, and Ryan is a manager without one. Ryan describes a graph from a company that gathers LinkedIn data, covering a few thousand directors and above. Pay with and without an MBA looked comparable, and pay without one was slightly lower. Ryan describes this as research done with a company, not a published study.

followups.question: Did family expectations about an MBA affect Ricky?
answer: Ricky's mother believed Ricky would not succeed without an MBA, and pushed for a top school. She has become more relaxed since Ricky reached staff engineer, and now reads about careers and thinks the path is good.
followups.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What was college recruiting like?
answer: Ricky says it was hard. Ricky describes a 15-minute coding challenge from Yelp, written in C++ on the merge step of a merge sort. The code looked right, but it kept crashing with a segmentation fault that Ricky could not explain, and Ricky was rejected. Ricky emailed the recruiter, insisted the code was correct, and asked for an engineer to check it. The engineer said the code looked correct. Ricky got another challenge, passed it, and reached the interview round. Ricky's lesson is that it is worth pushing back and advocating for yourself during recruiting.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Is the first job the hardest to land?
answer: Ryan says yes. The first role is the hardest, new grads have to be scrappy, and later offers get easier. Taking less desirable companies can build experience. Ricky says Ricky's first role was at a little-known company that Ricky no longer lists on the resume, but it made the next application look stronger and opened the door to better companies.

blocks.question: How do you make as much money as possible?
answer: Ryan says it depends on the goal. For very large wealth, the usual path is a few years in big tech, then a company of one's own, or an early join at a company that grows fast. Ryan says that for a good life, with money for the things you want and for vacations, big tech and good work are enough.

Ricky says reaching that level of wealth would take the two speakers decades of promotions, plus a rising market. Ricky says that, for a good life, big tech and a solid job are enough. Ricky had no real idea about money in college.

blocks.question: Is work the most important part of life?
answer: Ricky says work is not everything. Looking back at their 20s, Ricky's happiest memories were time with friends and trips, not working or getting promoted. Ricky says people should work hard and also build a life beyond work. Someone whose whole identity is their job can struggle after a layoff, while a person with other interests can handle it more easily.

followups.question: Can work-life balance be framed as diminishing returns?
answer: One speaker describes diminishing returns: each extra effort in one area gives smaller gains, so a person who wants the most out of life should look for areas where returns are still growing. The speaker says this favors spreading effort across several parts of life.

blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: What are your goals now, and did you push for promotion?
answer: Ricky says Ricky was not very career-driven at first. Ricky and Ryan were roommates and still are. Ryan would ask whether they could aim for promotion faster than the usual timeline. Ricky had seen data on how long each level took, and Ryan's push made Ricky test whether a faster path was possible.
Ricky says Ricky put in the effort, was promoted faster than average, and did not give up other interests to do it.
blocks.speaker: Ricky

blocks.question: Should people change jobs every two or three years for pay or promotion?
answer: Ricky says the answer depends on the case. Ricky has stayed on the same team under the same manager at Google, while still looking at other teams. Ricky notes survivorship bias, because people who left may have had a worse time. Ricky suggests asking every six months whether you still want to be there, whether the opportunities still fit, and whether the team and manager support you.

Ryan says the common advice to job hop for promotion is more nuanced. Early in a career, job hopping can be the fastest route, because momentum matters less than reaching the next level. At senior levels it can backfire. Ryan says companies usually do not hire outside candidates straight into E7 or L7, and promotion there depends on credibility and a track record that frequent moves do not build. Ryan's advice is to job hop aggressively early and to be more deliberate later.

followups.question: Can leaving a company help someone come back at a higher level?
answer: Ryan says this is rare. Ryan has seen a person leave a company, join a startup, and come back to Meta at a higher level. Ryan says a person who leaves a clear ladder is harder to place, so a return can leave room for a higher offer, but few cases work this way.
followups.speaker: Ryan

blocks.question: Will AI reduce entry-level software engineering jobs?
answer: The speakers say it is hard to predict five to ten years ahead. In the short term, they expect AI to change things less than many fear. They note that engineers already use many non-AI tools that write code, and that this did not scare anyone. They see AI as a tool that empowers engineers. Their advice is not to change majors only because of job fears.

followups.question: What might entry-level work look like in five to ten years?
answer: One speaker says entry-level engineers may write less code, because AI will do more of it. They will still need to tell the AI what to build and check that the result is correct. The speaker expects AI to remain a tool, and people will still be needed to build it.
